theory.title: Data & variables
theory.outcome: Classify variables as quantitative (discrete / continuous) or qualitative (nominal / ordinal).
theory.why: Data does not analyze itself. The **type of variable** decides which summary, which graph, which distribution and — later — which test you are allowed to use. Every exam question silently starts with this classification.
theory.definition:
- **Quantitative** variables represent numerical values. **Discrete**: isolated counts (number of siblings, number of courses). **Continuous**: measurements on a continuous scale (StudyHoursPerWeek, SleepHoursPerNight, FinalGrade).
- **Qualitative** (categorical) variables describe categories. **Nominal**: no natural order (StudyMethod, Gender, PartTimeJob). **Ordinal**: meaningful ranking (StressLevel: Low < Medium < High).
theory.example: In the 60-student dataset: *Age* is quantitative (in years — recorded as whole numbers, but age is conceptually continuous), *StudyHoursPerWeek* and *SleepHoursPerNight* are continuous, *StudyMethod* (Solo, Group, Tutoring, OnlineResources) is nominal, *StressLevel* is ordinal, *PassFail* is nominal (binary).
mistakes: Calling a variable "quantitative" because it is coded with numbers (e.g. 1 = Solo, 2 = Group). Codes are labels, not quantities.
Computing a mean of a categorical variable. For StressLevel or StudyMethod you can only report the **mode** (and frequencies).
Treating "number of siblings" as continuous — it can only take integer values, so it is discrete.
theory.examTip: Quiz 2 asked exactly this as True/False: "StressLevel is ordinal, StudyMethod is nominal" (True) and "we cannot compute a mean for categorical variables, but their mode can be identified" (True).

think.q: FinalGrade is used to create PassFail (pass mark 50). What happens to the information when you go from FinalGrade to PassFail?
think.a: You turn a continuous variable into a binary nominal one — information is lost (a 51 and a 94 become the same "Pass"). Methods for proportions (π) replace methods for means (μ).

think.q: Why does the variable type matter for choosing ANOVA vs. a chi-square test later?
think.a: ANOVA needs a metric (quantitative) dependent variable and a categorical factor; the chi-square test of independence needs two categorical variables. Classifying correctly is step 1 of the "Analytical Pipeline".

theory.title: Random variables
theory.outcome: Define a random variable and distinguish discrete from continuous random variables.
theory.why: A random variable lets us **describe uncertainty mathematically**: it turns the outcome of a random process (draw a student at random) into a number, so that we can attach probabilities to it.
theory.definition:
A **random variable** $X$ assigns a number to each outcome of a random process.
- **Discrete**: takes isolated values, each with a specific probability $P(X = x)$.
- **Continuous**: defined by a **probability density function** $f(x)$; probabilities are **areas under the curve**.
theory.example: Pick a Nova SBE student at random from the 60. $X$ = SleepHoursPerNight is a continuous random variable: $P(6.5 < X < 7.5)$ is the area under the density between 6.5 and 7.5.
mistakes: Asking for $P(X = 7)$ for a continuous variable and expecting a positive number — it is 0.
Worrying about "<" vs "≤" for continuous variables: $P(X < x) = P(X \le x)$.
theory.examTip: All four course tables give a **cumulative (left-tail) probability** $P[X < x]$ — the area to the left of $x$.

theory.title: Descriptive statistics: centre and spread
theory.outcome: Compute and interpret mean, median, mode, variance and standard deviation.
theory.why: Before any inference we summarise: **where** is the centre of the data and **how much** do values vary around it? Spread is what later drives standard errors, margins of error and test statistics.
theory.definition:
- **Mean**: the balance point (sensitive to extreme values).
- **Median**: the middle value of the ordered data — 50 % of the values lie below it.
- **Mode**: most frequent value/category (the only centre for nominal data).
- **Variance**: average squared deviation from the mean. **Standard deviation**: its square root, in the original units. Both are **non-negative**.
theory.example: Dataset (60 students): mean Age = **20.1**, median Age = **20**; median FinalGrade = **68.5**, i.e. *50 % of the final grades are below 68.5*. Treating the 60 students as the population: variance of StudyHoursPerWeek = **10.9** (VAR.P), SD of SleepHoursPerNight = **0.85** (STDEV.P). With the sample formulas you would get 11.1 and 0.86.
mistakes: Mixing population (÷N) and sample (÷(n−1)) formulas. In Quiz 2 the 60 students were treated as the **population** (answers 10.9 and 0.85 match VAR.P / STDEV.P).
Reporting the median as "50 % of grades ARE 68.5" — correct: 50 % are **below** 68.5.
Forgetting to square-root: SD and variance are in different units (hours vs hours²).
Ignoring the requested number of decimals. Moodle marked 10.89 wrong when "1 decimal digit" was asked (correct: 10.9).
theory.examTip: Read the rounding instruction twice. "use 1 decimal digit" → 10.9, not 10.89. "no decimals" → 20.

think.q: Why can variance and standard deviation never be negative?
think.a: They are built from squared deviations (≥ 0) divided by a positive number; the SD is the non-negative square root. A variance of 0 means all values are identical.

think.q: Why do we divide by n − 1 for a sample?
think.a: Deviations are measured from x̄, which is itself estimated from the same data, so they are slightly too small. Dividing by n − 1 (the degrees of freedom) corrects this and makes s² an unbiased estimator of σ².

theory.title: Other measures & skewness
theory.outcome: Use quartiles, range and IQR; read skewness from the relation between mean and median.
theory.why: Two variables can share the same mean and SD and still look completely different. **Shape** (symmetry, tails, outliers) tells you whether the mean is a good summary and whether normal-based methods are reasonable.
theory.definition:
- **Range** = max − min. **Quartiles** Q1, Q3 split the ordered data into quarters; **IQR** = Q3 − Q1 (the middle 50 %).
- **Skewness**: *right (positive) skew* → long tail to the right, typically **mean > median**; *left (negative) skew* → long tail to the left, **mean < median**; symmetric → mean ≈ median.
- **Outlier rule** (boxplot): below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR.
formulas: \text{outlier if } x < Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR} \ \text{ or } \ x > Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}
theory.example: FinalGrade: mean 67.2 < median 68.5 and Excel SKEW = −0.26 → slight **left** skew. AttendancePercent: SKEW = −0.73 (a few students with low attendance pull the tail to the left). Q1 and Q3 of FinalGrade: 57.75 and 78.25, IQR = 20.5.
mistakes: Naming the skew after the hump instead of the tail. The **tail** gives the direction.
Thinking skewness changes the median a lot — the median is robust; the **mean** moves toward the tail.
theory.examTip: If an exam asks "which is the better measure of centre for a strongly skewed variable?", answer the **median** (robust to the tail).

theory.title: Population vs. sample
theory.outcome: Distinguish population parameters from sample statistics and use the right notation.
theory.why: Inference = using a **sample statistic** (which we can compute) to learn about a **population parameter** (which we cannot see). Notation tells the reader which one you mean — examiners check it.
theory.definition:
Population **parameter** vs. sample **statistic**:
- Mean: $\mu$ vs. $\bar x$
- Standard deviation: $\sigma$ vs. $s$
- Variance: $\sigma^2$ vs. $s^2$
- Proportion: $\pi$ vs. $p$
- Size: $N$ vs. $n$

A **parameter** is fixed but unknown; a **statistic** varies from sample to sample (sampling variability).
theory.example: The 60 Nova SBE students can be seen as a **sample** of all Nova master students (then $\bar x = 67.2$ estimates $\mu$) or as the **population** of interest (then 67.2 *is* $\mu$). The research question decides.
mistakes: Writing hypotheses about $\bar x$ (e.g. $H_0: \bar x = 15$). Hypotheses are **always** about parameters: $H_0: \mu = 15$.
Using $p$ for the population proportion — the course uses $\pi$ for the population and $p$ for the sample.
theory.examTip: Every hypothesis and every CI statement must mention a **parameter** ($\mu$ or $\pi$, …).

theory.title: Distributions: Normal, t-Student, χ², F
theory.outcome: Describe the shape, centre and spread of the Standard Normal, t-Student, Chi-square and F-Snedecor distributions.
theory.why: Each test statistic in this course follows one of four distributions. Knowing their shapes tells you **where the rejection region is** and **whether the symmetry trick works**.
theory.definition:
- **Standard Normal Z**: symmetric bell, mean 0, SD 1. Fixed universal shape.
- **t-Student**: symmetric bell with **heavier tails**, mean 0, SD > 1. Shape depends on the **degrees of freedom**; as df → ∞ it becomes Z.
- **Chi-square χ²**: not symmetric, **skewed to the right**, only positive values; shape depends on df, more symmetric as df grows.
- **F-Snedecor**: right-skewed, positive; depends on **two** df (numerator $m$, denominator $n$).
theory.example: Compare the last row of the t table (df = ∞) with the Z table: $t_{0.975,\infty} = 1.960 = z_{0.975}$ and $t_{0.95,\infty} = 1.645 = z_{0.95}$.
mistakes: Using symmetry ($-$value) for χ² or F. They are not symmetric — lower-tail values must be read from their own columns.
Forgetting that t has heavier tails: for small samples the t critical value is **larger** than z.
theory.examTip: Course summary table: Z — symmetric, mean 0, SD 1, df no impact; t — symmetric heavy tails, mean 0, SD > 1, df determines tail thickness; χ² — right-skewed, df drives shape toward symmetry; F — right-skewed, driven by two df.

think.q: Why does the t distribution need degrees of freedom while Z does not?
think.a: t accounts for the extra uncertainty from estimating σ with s. With few observations s is unreliable → heavier tails. The more df, the better s estimates σ and the closer t gets to Z.

theory.title: Reading the statistical tables
theory.outcome: Use the Z, t, χ² and F tables to go from score to probability and from probability to score.
theory.why: The exam is open-book and AI can compute anything — but the course expects you to **read the tables manually** and understand what you read. Every critical value and many p-values come from here.
theory.definition:
All four course tables are **left-tail cumulative**: the number in the table is $p = P[X < x]$.
- **Z table**: row = first decimal of z, column = second decimal; cell = $P[Z < z]$. Only positive z — use symmetry $P(Z < -z) = 1 - P(Z < z)$.
- **t table**: row = df, column = probability $P[t_{df} < t]$ (0.999 … 0.500); cell = t score.
- **χ² table**: row = df, column = $P[\chi^2_{df} < q]$ (0.005 … 0.995); cell = q.
- **F table**: blocks by $n$ (denominator df), rows inside a block = probability (0.900 … 0.995), columns = $m$ (numerator df); cell = f.
formulas: P(a < Z < b) = P(Z < b) - P(Z < a)
P(T > t) = p \iff P(T < t) = 1 - p
mistakes: "Above" vs "below": $P(T > t) = 0.975$ is a value **below** zero. Draw the curve and shade the area first.
Looking up α instead of $1 - \alpha$ (or $1 - \alpha/2$). For a right-tail critical value at α = 0.05 use column **0.950**.
Swapping F degrees of freedom: $m$ = numerator (columns), $n$ = denominator (blocks).
Applying symmetry to χ² / F.
theory.examTip: Moodle grades the number of decimals strictly: **−2.131** was marked wrong when 2 decimals were requested (−2.13). Quiz 2 also said: use the tables first and *only after* confirm with AI.

think.q: df = 39 is not a row in the t table. What do you do?
think.a: Use the closest available row (df = 40) or, to be conservative, the smaller one (df = 30). The difference is small (2.021 vs 2.042). In the exam you can confirm with Excel T.INV(0.975; 39) = 2.023.

think.q: Why does the χ² table have columns both near 0 (0.005) and near 1 (0.995)?
think.a: Because χ² is not symmetric — a lower-tail value cannot be obtained from an upper-tail value by changing the sign. Both tails need their own columns.

theory.title: Standardising a normal variable
theory.outcome: Convert X ~ N(μ, σ) into Z and compute probabilities with the Z table.
theory.why: There is only one Z table, but infinitely many normal distributions. Standardising maps any normal variable onto Z so the same table answers every question.
theory.definition: If $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma)$ then $Z = (X-\mu)/\sigma \sim N(0,1)$. The z score says **how many standard deviations** $x$ lies above (+) or below (−) the mean.
mistakes: Dividing by the variance instead of the standard deviation.
Rounding z to 1 decimal — the Z table works with 2 decimals.
theory.examTip: Round z to **2 decimals** before reading the Z table; report probabilities with 4 decimals unless told otherwise.

theory.title: Sampling and representativeness
theory.outcome: Explain random sampling, representativeness and sampling variability.
theory.why: We almost never observe the whole population (all Nova students). A sample is only useful if it **represents** the population — otherwise no formula can rescue the conclusion.
theory.definition:
- **Simple random sample**: every member of the population has the same chance of being selected, independently.
- **Representative sample**: its composition mirrors the population on relevant characteristics.
- **Sampling variability**: different samples give different statistics ($\bar x$, $p$, $s$) — purely by chance.
- **Bias** (systematic error) does not shrink with larger n; **random error** does.
theory.example: Surveying only students in the library on a Sunday evening would over-represent heavy studiers: StudyHoursPerWeek would be **biased upwards**, however many students you ask.
mistakes: Thinking a large sample fixes a biased sampling method.
Confusing sampling variability (natural, quantifiable) with bias (systematic, not fixed by n).
theory.examTip: If a question asks why two samples give different means, the keyword is **sampling variability**.

think.q: Two classmates each take a random sample of 30 students and get x̄ = 9.1 and x̄ = 9.6 study hours. Did one of them make a mistake?
think.a: No. Different random samples give different means — sampling variability. The sampling distribution of x̄ describes how large these differences typically are (its SD is the standard error).

theory.title: Sampling distribution of x̄ and the standard error
theory.outcome: Describe the sampling distribution of the sample mean and compute the standard error.
theory.why: To know how far $\bar x$ can be from $\mu$, we need the distribution of $\bar x$ over all possible samples. Its spread — the **standard error** — is the building block of every CI and test.
theory.definition:
If we repeatedly draw samples of size n and compute $\bar x$ each time, the values of $\bar x$ form the **sampling distribution of the mean**:
- centre: $E(\bar X) = \mu$ (x̄ is unbiased)
- spread: $SE = \sigma/\sqrt n$ (estimated by $s/\sqrt n$)
- larger n → smaller SE → $\bar x$ closer to $\mu$. To **halve** the SE you need **4×** the sample size.
theory.example: StudyHoursPerWeek: σ ≈ 3.3. With n = 36: SE = 3.3/6 = 0.55 hours. With n = 144: SE = 3.3/12 = 0.275 hours (half).
mistakes: Using σ instead of σ/√n when the question is about the **mean** of a sample.
Confusing SD (spread of individual students) with SE (spread of sample means).
theory.examTip: Excel "Descriptive Statistics" prints **Standard Error** = s/√n — that is the SE of the mean, not the SD.

theory.title: The Central Limit Theorem (must-know!)
theory.outcome: State the CLT and use it to compute probabilities about x̄.
theory.why: The lecturer marks the CLT as **mandatory**: it is the reason we can use the normal (and t) distribution for means even when the data themselves are not normal.
theory.definition:
For a random sample of size n from **any** population with mean μ and SD σ, the sampling distribution of $\bar X$ is **approximately normal** when n is large enough (rule of thumb **n ≥ 30**): $\bar X \approx N(\mu, \sigma/\sqrt n)$.
- If the population is itself normal, $\bar X$ is exactly normal for any n.
- The more skewed the population, the larger n must be.
theory.example:
AttendancePercent is left-skewed (SKEW −0.73). Still, the mean attendance of random groups of 40 students is approximately normal with mean μ and SE = σ/√40.

P(x̄ > 10) for StudyHours with μ = 9.3, σ = 3.3, n = 36: $z = (10-9.3)/0.55 = 1.27$ → $1 - 0.8980 = 0.1020$.
mistakes: Saying the CLT makes the **data** normal. It is about the distribution of the **sample mean**.
Applying the CLT with n = 8 from a strongly skewed population.
Forgetting √n in the denominator.
theory.examTip: Typical exam sentence: *"By the CLT, since n ≥ 30, the sampling distribution of x̄ is approximately normal with mean μ and standard error σ/√n."*

think.q: Why does averaging make a skewed distribution look normal?
think.a: Extreme values in one direction tend to be balanced by ordinary values when you average many independent observations. Sums of many independent pieces pile up around the middle — the bell shape.

think.q: What happens to the sampling distribution of x̄ as n → ∞?
think.a: It concentrates around μ (SE → 0) and becomes ever closer to normal.

theory.title: Point estimation and good estimators
theory.outcome: Name point estimators for μ, σ and π and the properties of good estimators.
theory.why: Before building intervals we need a single best guess. Not every formula is a good guess — estimators are judged by objective properties.
theory.definition:
- **Point estimate**: a single number from the sample used to estimate a parameter: $\bar x \to \mu$, $s \to \sigma$, $p \to \pi$.
- **Unbiased**: the sampling distribution is centred on the parameter ($E(\bar X)=\mu$; $s^2$ with n−1 is unbiased for $\sigma^2$).
- **Efficient**: smallest variance among unbiased estimators.
- **Consistent**: gets closer to the parameter as n grows.
theory.example: 49 of 60 students passed: point estimate of the pass rate $p = 49/60 = 0.817$. It says nothing about its own precision — that is why we need a CI.
mistakes: Reporting only a point estimate when the question asks about precision/uncertainty.
theory.examTip: A point estimate is **never** exactly equal to the parameter; the CI quantifies how far off it may be.

theory.title: Confidence interval for μ
theory.outcome: Construct a CI for the mean with Z (σ known) or t (σ unknown) and identify the reliability factor and margin of error.
theory.why: A CI turns a point estimate into a statement about precision: a range of plausible values for μ, with a stated confidence level.
theory.definition:
**Point estimate ± margin of error**, where margin of error = **reliability factor × standard error**.
- σ known (or n large, course convention): reliability factor $z_{1-\alpha/2}$.
- σ unknown: $t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}$ with **df = n − 1**.
- Confidence level $1-\alpha$: 90 % → 1.645; 95 % → 1.96; 99 % → 2.576 (Z).
mistakes: Using z when σ is unknown and n is small.
Using column 0.95 for a 95 % two-sided CI — the correct column is **0.975** (α/2 in each tail).
Wrong df (n instead of n − 1).
theory.examTip: Write the reliability factor with its table location: "$t_{0.975;15} = 2.131$ (t table, row 15, column 0.975)".

think.q: Why does the t reliability factor shrink towards 1.96 as n grows?
think.a: With more data, s becomes a reliable estimate of σ, so the extra uncertainty disappears and the t distribution converges to Z (last row of the t table = Z values).

theory.title: Margin of error: n, variability, confidence level
theory.outcome: Explain how sample size, variability and confidence level affect the width of a CI; compute the required n.
theory.why: In practice you design the study: how many students must you survey for a given precision? And the exam loves "what happens to the interval if…" questions.
theory.definition:
- **n ↑** → SE ↓ → narrower CI (width ∝ 1/√n).
- **Variability σ ↑** → wider CI.
- **Confidence level ↑** (95 % → 99 %) → larger reliability factor → wider CI. More confidence costs precision.
- **Precision**: 15.0 ± 0.2 is much more precise than 15.0 ± 1.5 (same centre, smaller ME).
theory.example: To estimate mean sleep (σ = 0.85) within ±0.2 h at 95 %: $n = (1.96 \cdot 0.85/0.2)^2 = 69.4$ → **70 students**.
mistakes: Rounding the required n down — always round **up**.
Thinking a 99 % CI is "more precise" than a 95 % CI — it is wider, so less precise.
theory.examTip: Width = 2 × ME. If you are given an interval [a; b]: centre = (a+b)/2, ME = (b−a)/2.

theory.title: Confidence interval for a proportion π
theory.outcome: Construct and interpret a CI for a population proportion.
theory.why: Many questions are about shares: pass rate, share of students with a part-time job. The logic is identical to μ — only the SE changes.
theory.definition: With sample proportion $p = x/n$ and a large sample ($np \ge 5$ and $n(1-p) \ge 5$), the reliability factor is **always z**.
mistakes: Using t for proportions.
Using percentages (81.67) inside the square root instead of proportions (0.8167).
theory.examTip: State the condition np ≥ 5 and n(1−p) ≥ 5 in one line — examiners reward it.

theory.title: Interpreting a confidence interval correctly
theory.outcome: Interpret a 95 % CI correctly and recognise common misinterpretations.
theory.why: Interpretation is where most exam points are lost — the computation is the easy part.
theory.definition:
**Correct**: "We are 95 % confident that the interval [14.36; 15.64] contains the **population mean** GPA μ." Meaning: if we repeated the sampling many times, about 95 % of the intervals built this way would contain μ.

**Wrong**:
- "There is a 95 % probability that μ lies in [14.36; 15.64]" (μ is fixed; this interval either contains it or not).
- "95 % of students have a GPA between 14.36 and 15.64" (CI is about the mean, not individuals).
- "95 % of sample means fall in this interval."
theory.example: The CI simulator draws 100 intervals: roughly 95 of them cover μ, about 5 miss it — and you never know which ones.
mistakes: Talking about x̄ in the interpretation (x̄ is always in the centre of its own CI).
Forgetting the context (units, population).
theory.examTip: Template: *"We are (1−α)·100 % confident that the population mean [variable, units] of [population] lies between a and b."*

think.q: Does a 95 % CI that contains μ₀ = 15 prove that μ = 15?
think.a: No. It only says 15 is a plausible value — many other values in the interval are equally plausible. (This is the CI ↔ test link of World 3: "fail to reject" ≠ "accept".)

theory.title: Null and alternative hypotheses
theory.outcome: Formulate H₀ and H₁ about μ or π and choose a left-, right- or two-tailed test.
theory.why: A test can only answer the question you asked. Wrong hypotheses = wrong tail = wrong conclusion, even with perfect arithmetic. This is where the exam checks your logic.
theory.definition:
- **H₀** (null): the status quo / the claim being tested, always contains **equality** ($=$, $\le$, $\ge$).
- **H₁** (alternative): what we want to find evidence for; determines the tail.
- **Two-tailed**: $H_1: \mu \ne \mu_0$ ("differs from"). **Right-tailed**: $H_1: \mu > \mu_0$ ("more than"). **Left-tailed**: $H_1: \mu < \mu_0$ ("less than").
theory.example:
- Claim "students study **5 hours per day** on average": $H_0: \mu = 5$ vs $H_1: \mu \ne 5$.
- "The mean GPA is **higher than 15**": $H_0: \mu \le 15$ vs $H_1: \mu > 15$ (right-tailed).
- "Students sleep **less than 7 hours**": $H_0: \mu \ge 7$ vs $H_1: \mu < 7$ (left-tailed).
mistakes: Writing hypotheses with x̄ instead of μ.
Putting the equality in H₁.
Choosing the tail after looking at the data.
theory.examTip: Translate the words: "differs / changed" → ≠; "exceeds / more / increased" → >; "less / decreased / below" → <.

think.q: Why does the equality always sit in H₀?
think.a: The test statistic is computed assuming H₀ is true, so H₀ must specify one concrete value (μ₀) to centre the sampling distribution on.

theory.title: The testing procedure step by step
theory.outcome: Carry out a complete test: hypotheses → α → test statistic → critical value / p-value → decision → conclusion.
theory.why: Exam answers are graded step by step. A fixed routine makes sure you never skip the step that carries the points (often the conclusion sentence).
theory.definition:
1. State $H_0$ and $H_1$.
2. Choose the significance level **α** (usually 0.05).
3. Compute the **test statistic** (z or t) from the sample.
4. Find the **critical value** from the table → rejection region (or compute the **p-value**).
5. **Decision rule**: reject $H_0$ if the statistic falls in the rejection region (⇔ p-value < α).
6. **Conclusion** in context, in plain English.
theory.example: Course example: n = 40, x̄ = 15.8, μ₀ = 15, s = 2.4, α = 0.05, two-tailed: $t = 0.8/(2.4/\sqrt{40}) = 2.11$; critical value $t_{0.975;39} \approx 2.021$ (row 40) → 2.11 > 2.021 → reject H₀: the mean GPA differs significantly from 15.
mistakes: Stopping at "reject H₀" without a conclusion in context.
Comparing the test statistic with α (compare statistic with critical value, or p-value with α).
theory.examTip: Always end with: *"At the 5 % significance level, there is (not) sufficient evidence to conclude that …"*

theory.title: Critical values and rejection regions
theory.outcome: Read the correct critical value (z or t) for each type of test and write the decision rule.
theory.why: The rejection region turns α into a concrete cut-off. Reading the right table column is a classic exam trap — especially with the left-tail course tables.
theory.definition:
With the course (left-tail) tables:
- **Right-tailed**: reject if stat > critical value at column **1 − α** (α = 0.05 → 0.950: z = 1.645).
- **Left-tailed**: reject if stat < −(value at column 1 − α) (z = −1.645).
- **Two-tailed**: reject if |stat| > value at column **1 − α/2** (α = 0.05 → 0.975: z = 1.96).
- **z or t?** σ known → z; σ unknown → t with df = n − 1 (large n: t ≈ z).
theory.example: α = 0.05, n = 16, σ unknown, left-tailed → $t_{0.95;15} = 1.753$ → reject if t < −1.753.
mistakes: Using 1.96 for a one-tailed test at 5 % (correct: 1.645).
Forgetting the minus sign for left-tailed tests.
theory.examTip: Write the decision rule *before* computing the statistic: "Reject H₀ if t < −1.753."

links.label: See rejection regions in the Lab

theory.title: The p-value and its misconceptions
theory.outcome: Compute or bracket a p-value with the tables and interpret it correctly.
theory.why: Software reports p-values, not critical values. You must be able to read them — and to bracket them with the t table when no software is allowed.
theory.definition:
**p-value** = probability, **assuming H₀ is true**, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.
- Right-tailed: $P(Z > z_{obs})$; left: $P(Z < z_{obs})$; two-tailed: $2\,P(Z > |z_{obs}|)$.
- Reject H₀ if **p-value < α**. Same decision as the critical-value method — always.
- With the t table you can only **bracket** p: e.g. t = 2.35, df = 10 lies between 2.228 (0.975) and 2.764 (0.990) → one tail 0.01–0.025 → two-tailed **0.02 < p < 0.05**.
mistakes: "p is the probability that H₀ is true." — No, p is computed *assuming* H₀ is true.
"p > α proves H₀." — No, it only means insufficient evidence against H₀.
Forgetting to double the one-tail area for two-tailed tests.
theory.examTip: Small p = data are surprising if H₀ were true → evidence against H₀.

think.q: A study reports p = 0.03. A friend says "so there is a 3 % chance the null hypothesis is true". Correct them.
think.a: The p-value is P(data at least this extreme | H₀ true), not P(H₀ true | data). It measures how surprising the data are under H₀, not the probability of H₀.

theory.title: Type I and Type II errors, power
theory.outcome: Define Type I and Type II errors, power, and explain the influence of α and n.
theory.why: Every decision can be wrong. Knowing which error you risk — and how to control it — is core statistical literacy and a favourite conceptual exam question.
theory.definition:
- **Type I error**: reject H₀ when H₀ is true. P(Type I) = **α**.
- **Type II error**: do not reject H₀ when H₀ is false. P(Type II) = **β**.
- **Power** = 1 − β = P(reject H₀ | H₀ false).
- α ↓ → β ↑ (for fixed n). **n ↑** → SE ↓ → power ↑ (both errors can be reduced). Larger true effect → more power.
mistakes: Mixing up the two errors: Type I = "false alarm", Type II = "missed detection".
Thinking a lower α is always better (it raises β).
theory.examTip: Memory hook: **Type I = I**nnocent convicted (H₀ true, rejected).

theory.title: Statistical vs. practical significance; "fail to reject"
theory.outcome: Distinguish statistical from practical significance and phrase non-rejection correctly.
theory.why: With n = 10 000 even a 0.05-point GPA difference is "significant". Decision makers care whether the effect matters — and examiners check that you do not "accept" H₀.
theory.definition:
- **Statistical significance**: the effect is unlikely to be due to chance (p < α).
- **Practical significance**: the effect is large enough to matter in context.
- **"Fail to reject H₀" ≠ "accept H₀"**: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence (maybe n was too small).
theory.example: Mean GPA 15.08 vs μ₀ = 15 with n = 5 000 could be statistically significant, yet 0.08 points on a 20-point scale is practically irrelevant.
mistakes: Writing "we accept H₀" or "H₀ is true".
Equating "significant" with "important".
theory.examTip: Phrase: *"We do not reject H₀; the data do not provide sufficient evidence that μ differs from 15."*

theory.title: Confidence intervals ↔ two-tailed tests
theory.outcome: Use a CI to decide a two-tailed test and explain why both give the same answer.
theory.why: If you already have the CI, you can decide a two-tailed test instantly — a very common exam shortcut.
theory.definition: A two-tailed test at level α rejects $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ **exactly when** μ₀ lies **outside** the $(1-\alpha)$ CI. Both use the same estimate, SE and reliability factor.
theory.example: 95 % CI for mean GPA: [14.36; 15.64]. Test H₀: μ = 15 at α = 0.05 → 15 is inside → do not reject. Test H₀: μ = 16 → 16 is outside → reject.
mistakes: Using a 95 % CI for a test at α = 0.01 (need the 99 % CI).
Using a two-sided CI to decide a one-tailed test without adjusting.

theory.title: Testing a proportion π
theory.outcome: Test a claim about a population proportion with the z statistic.
theory.why: Pass rates, market shares, "more than half of students…": proportions are everywhere and follow the same 6-step logic.
theory.definition:
For $H_0: \pi = \pi_0$ and large n ($n\pi_0 \ge 5$, $n(1-\pi_0) \ge 5$):
$$z = \frac{p - \pi_0}{\sqrt{\pi_0(1-\pi_0)/n}}$$
Note: the SE uses **π₀** (the value under H₀), unlike the CI, which uses p.
theory.example: Claim: at least 90 % pass. Data: 49/60 = 0.8167. $H_0: \pi \ge 0.9$ vs $H_1: \pi < 0.9$. $z = (0.8167 - 0.9)/\sqrt{0.9 \cdot 0.1/60} = -2.15$ → p = 1 − 0.9842 = 0.0158 < 0.05 → reject: the pass rate is significantly below 90 %.
mistakes: Using p instead of π₀ in the test SE.
Using t for proportions.
theory.examTip: CI for π: SE with p. Test for π: SE with π₀.

theory.title: Why ANOVA and not many t-tests?
theory.outcome: Explain why comparing k means requires ANOVA instead of repeated t-tests.
theory.why: Does mean GPA differ between Solo, Group, Hybrid (or Tutoring, Online) study methods? With 4 groups you would need 6 pairwise t-tests — and the chance of at least one false alarm explodes.
theory.definition: With m independent tests at α = 0.05, the probability of **at least one Type I error** (family-wise error) is $1 - 0.95^m$. ANOVA tests all means **at once** with a single test at level α.
theory.example: 4 study methods → 6 pairs → $1 - 0.95^6 = 0.265$: a 26.5 % chance of declaring a difference that does not exist.
mistakes: Running many t-tests and reporting the "significant" one.
Thinking ANOVA compares variances as the research question — it compares **means**, using variances as a tool.
theory.examTip: Typical question: "Why not t-tests?" → inflated Type I error (family-wise error rate).

theory.title: Set-up, hypotheses and assumptions
theory.outcome: Identify the dependent variable and factor; state H₀/H₁ and the assumptions of one-way ANOVA.
theory.why: ANOVA is only the right tool for one combination of variable types. Check the types first (World 1!).
theory.definition:
- **Dependent variable**: metric (quantitative), e.g. FinalGrade, GPA, Stress score.
- **Factor**: categorical with k ≥ 2 groups, e.g. StudyMethod, StressLevel.
- $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_k$ — all population means equal.
- $H_1$: **at least one** mean differs (not "all differ"!).
- Assumptions: independent random samples, normal populations (or large groups), **equal variances** (homogeneity).
theory.example: FinalGrade (metric) by StudyMethod (nominal, k = 4): $H_0: \mu_{Solo} = \mu_{Group} = \mu_{Tutoring} = \mu_{Online}$.
mistakes: H₁: "all means are different" — wrong; one difference is enough.
Using ANOVA with a categorical dependent variable (that is a χ² problem).
theory.examTip: ANOVA: metric ~ categorical. χ²: categorical ~ categorical. Regression: metric ~ metric.

theory.title: Between vs. within variability: SST = SSB + SSW
theory.outcome: Decompose total variability into between-group and within-group sums of squares.
theory.why: The key idea: if group means differ, the spread **between** group means is large compared to the natural spread **within** groups.
theory.definition:
- **SST** (total): variation of all observations around the grand mean $\bar{\bar x}$.
- **SSB** (between / treatment): variation of the group means around the grand mean, weighted by group size.
- **SSW** (within / error): variation of observations around their own group mean.
theory.example: FinalGrade by StudyMethod: the Tutoring group (mean 84.5) is far from the others (60–65) → large SSB, while each group has SD 8–15 → moderate SSW.
mistakes: Forgetting the weights $n_j$ in SSB.
Computing SSW with n_j instead of (n_j − 1) when using group SDs.
theory.examTip: From summaries (n, mean, s per group): SSW = Σ(nⱼ−1)sⱼ² — very common in exams.

theory.title: Mean squares, the F statistic and the F table
theory.outcome: Compute MSB, MSW, F and its degrees of freedom; decide with the F table or p-value.
theory.why: Sums of squares grow with the number of terms; dividing by df makes them comparable. Their ratio F follows the F-Snedecor distribution under H₀.
theory.definition:
- $df_B = k - 1$, $df_W = n - k$, $df_T = n - 1$
- $MSB = SSB/(k-1)$, $MSW = SSW/(n-k)$
- $F = MSB/MSW$. Under H₀, F ≈ 1. Large F → evidence against H₀.
- **Always right-tailed**: reject H₀ if $F > F_{1-\alpha;\,k-1,\,n-k}$ (F table: column m = k − 1, block n = n − k, row 1 − α).
theory.example: 3 groups, n = 30 → df (2, 27). Critical value $F_{0.95;2,27} \approx 3.354$. Course table: block n = 27 is missing → use n = 30 (3.32) or compute with F.INV (3.354).
mistakes: Swapping the df: numerator = k − 1 (columns m), denominator = n − k (blocks n).
Using a two-tailed rejection region — ANOVA is always right-tailed.
theory.examTip: Write "$F_{0.95;\,(2,\,27)}$" with both df — the order matters.

think.q: Why is F close to 1 when H₀ is true?
think.a: Under H₀ both MSB and MSW estimate the same common variance σ², so their ratio fluctuates around 1. Only real differences between means inflate MSB.

theory.title: Reading and completing the ANOVA table
theory.outcome: Read software ANOVA tables and fill in missing cells.
theory.why: Exams love an ANOVA table with holes. Every cell follows from two or three others.
theory.definition:
Columns: Source · SS · df · MS · F · p-value.
- **Between groups**: SSB, k − 1, MSB, F, p
- **Within groups**: SSW, n − k, MSW
- **Total**: SST, n − 1

Rules: SS and df **add up** down the column; MS = SS/df; F = MSB/MSW. MS do **not** add up.
mistakes: Adding MS values to get a "total MS".
Taking F = SSB/SSW instead of MSB/MSW.
theory.examTip: Excel calls them "Between Groups / Within Groups"; Jamovi uses the factor name and "Residuals".

theory.title: After rejecting: post-hoc tests and links
theory.outcome: Explain what post-hoc tests do and how ANOVA links to regression.
theory.why: Rejecting H₀ only says "some mean differs". Which one? That is the job of post-hoc comparisons.
theory.definition:
- **Post-hoc tests** (e.g. Tukey, Bonferroni) compare all pairs while controlling the family-wise error rate.
- Only run them **after** a significant F.
- **Effect size** η² = SSB/SST: share of total variability explained by the factor.
- **Link**: the F test of a simple regression has the same logic (MSR/MSE) — "explained vs. unexplained" variability.
theory.example: GPA by study method: F significant; Tukey shows Tutoring differs from Solo, Group and Online, while the other three do not differ significantly.
mistakes: Running post-hoc tests when F was not significant.
Concluding "Tutoring causes higher grades" — observational data show association, not causation.
theory.examTip: Conclusion template: "At α = 0.05, there is sufficient evidence that the mean [Y] differs for at least one [factor] group."

theory.title: Contingency tables: joint, marginal and conditional
theory.outcome: Build a contingency table and compute joint, marginal and conditional relative frequencies.
theory.why: Is passing the course related to having a part-time job? Both variables are categorical — means make no sense, so we count.
theory.definition:
- A **contingency table** (cross table) counts observations for every combination of two categorical variables: r rows × c columns.
- **Marginal totals**: row totals and column totals; grand total n.
- **Joint** relative frequency: cell / n.
- **Conditional** relative frequency: cell / row total (row %) or cell / column total (column %).
theory.example: Dataset: PartTimeJob × PassFail. No job: 35 Pass, 0 Fail. Job: 14 Pass, 11 Fail. Conditional fail rate: 0 % without a job vs 11/25 = 44 % with a job — a striking difference.
mistakes: Comparing raw counts of groups with different sizes instead of conditional percentages.
Mixing up row % and column % — say which one you use.
theory.examTip: If the row-% profiles are (almost) identical across rows, the variables look independent.

think.q: If PassFail were independent of PartTimeJob, what would the fail rates look like in the two rows?
think.a: Equal (up to sampling noise): both rows would show the overall fail rate 11/60 ≈ 18.3 %.

theory.title: The χ² test of independence: hypotheses
theory.outcome: State H₀ and H₁ of the test of independence in context.
theory.why: Sample tables always show some differences. Are they bigger than random noise would produce?
theory.definition:
- $H_0$: the two variables are **independent** (no association) in the population.
- $H_1$: the two variables are **dependent** (associated).
- Equivalent wording: H₀: the conditional distribution of Y is the same in every category of X.
- Requires a random sample and counts (not percentages!).
theory.example: H₀: StudyMethod and PassFail are independent; H₁: StudyMethod and PassFail are associated.
mistakes: Writing hypotheses about means (μ) — the test is about independence.
Running the test on percentages instead of absolute counts.
theory.examTip: Always phrase H₀ with "independent" and H₁ with "associated / dependent" — and name both variables.

theory.title: Expected counts under independence
theory.outcome: Compute expected cell counts under H₀.
theory.why: Independence means P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B). Multiply by n and you get the count we would expect in each cell if H₀ were true.
theory.definition: For cell (i, j): expected count = row total × column total / grand total. Expected counts keep the same margins as the observed table.
theory.example: PartTimeJob = Yes (25 students) and Fail (11 students), n = 60: $E = 25 \cdot 11 / 60 = 4.58$. Observed: 11 — far more than expected.
mistakes: Rounding expected counts to integers — keep decimals.
Using row total × column total without dividing by n.
theory.examTip: Check: every row of expected counts sums to the observed row total.

theory.title: The χ² statistic, df and the decision rule
theory.outcome: Compute χ², its degrees of freedom and decide with the chi-square table or p-value.
theory.why: We need one number that measures how far the whole table is from independence.
theory.definition:
- $\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ over all r·c cells.
- $df = (r-1)(c-1)$.
- **Right-tailed**: reject H₀ if $\chi^2 > \chi^2_{1-\alpha;\,df}$ (chi-square table: row df, column 1 − α, e.g. 0.950).
- p-value = P(χ²_df > observed χ²) = 1 − CHISQ.DIST(x; df; TRUE) = CHISQ.DIST.RT.
theory.example: StressLevel (3) × PassFail (2): df = 2·1 = 2. Critical value at α = 0.05: 5.991. Observed χ² = 48.70 ≫ 5.991 → reject H₀.
mistakes: df = r·c − 1 or n − 1 — wrong; it is (r − 1)(c − 1).
Reading the 0.050 column instead of 0.950 in the left-tail course table.
theory.examTip: The course table is left-tail: for α = 0.05 use the column **0.950**. $\chi^2_{0.95;4} = 9.488$.

think.q: Why is the χ² test always right-tailed?
think.a: Because every deviation from independence — in any direction — makes (O − E)² larger. Only large values of χ² speak against H₀.

theory.title: Conditions: expected counts ≥ 5
theory.outcome: Check the validity condition and know what to do when it fails.
theory.why: The χ² distribution is only an approximation. With tiny expected counts it can be badly wrong.
theory.definition:
- Rule of thumb: **all expected counts ≥ 5** (some books: at most 20 % below 5 and none below 1).
- If violated: **merge categories** (e.g. Low + Medium stress) or collect more data; for 2×2 tables Fisher's exact test is an alternative.
- Condition concerns **expected**, not observed, counts.
theory.example: StudyMethod × PassFail: the Fail column has expected counts 3.12, 2.38, 2.75, 2.75 — all below 5. The χ² result (5.26, df 3) must be interpreted with caution; merging methods into "Tutoring vs other" helps.
mistakes: Checking observed counts (an observed 0 is fine if E ≥ 5).
Ignoring the warning in the conclusion.
theory.examTip: Exam questions often ask: "Is the test valid?" → compute the smallest expected count.

theory.title: Interpreting the result: contributions and association ≠ causation
theory.outcome: Identify the cells driving the result and write a correct conclusion without causal claims.
theory.why: Rejecting H₀ tells you that the variables are related, not how. The cell contributions show where the table deviates most.
theory.definition:
- **Cell contribution** $(O-E)^2/E$: large values show the cells that drive χ².
- Compare O with E in those cells: more or fewer than expected?
- Strength (optional): Cramér's $V = \sqrt{\chi^2/(n\,(\min(r,c)-1))}$, between 0 and 1.
- A significant association **does not imply causation** (confounders, reverse causality).
- Method choice: two categorical variables → χ²; metric by groups → ANOVA.
theory.example: PartTimeJob × PassFail: χ² = 18.86, df 1, p < 0.001. Largest contribution: Job/Fail (O = 11 vs E = 4.58). Working students fail more often — but stress, time and motivation may confound this.
mistakes: "Part-time jobs cause students to fail." — association only.
Concluding "strong association" just because p is tiny (p depends on n).
theory.examTip: Conclusion template: "At α = 0.05 there is sufficient evidence that X and Y are associated (not independent)."

theory.title: Scatter plots, covariance and correlation r
theory.outcome: Describe a linear relationship with a scatter plot, the covariance and Pearson's r.
theory.why: Do students who study more get better grades? With two metric variables, the first step is always a scatter plot.
theory.definition:
- **Covariance** $s_{xy}$: sign tells the direction (+ / −), but the size depends on units.
- **Pearson correlation** $r = s_{xy}/(s_x s_y)$, always between −1 and +1: strength and direction of the **linear** relationship.
- r ≈ 0 means no **linear** relation (there can still be a curved one).
theory.example: Dataset: StudyHoursPerWeek and FinalGrade have r = 0.993 — an extremely strong positive linear relationship (the data are cleaned teaching data; real data are rarely this tidy).
mistakes: Reading r = 0.3 as "30 % explained" — that is r² = 9 %.
Concluding causation from a high correlation.
theory.examTip: r has no units and is symmetric: corr(x, y) = corr(y, x). The regression slope is not symmetric.

theory.title: The least-squares line: b₀ and b₁
theory.outcome: Compute the OLS intercept and slope from raw data or summary statistics.
theory.why: Among all straight lines, we pick the one with the smallest sum of squared vertical errors (residuals).
theory.definition:
- Model: $Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \varepsilon$; estimated line $\hat y = b_0 + b_1 x$.
- OLS minimises $\sum e_i^2 = \sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2$.
- The line always passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$.
theory.example: Dataset: $\widehat{FinalGrade} = 25.17 + 4.524 \cdot StudyHoursPerWeek$.
mistakes: Swapping x and y (regressing x on y gives a different line).
Computing b₀ before b₁ — b₀ needs b₁.
theory.examTip: From summaries: b₁ = r·s_y/s_x, then b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄. Keep 4+ decimals in intermediate steps.

think.q: Why squared residuals and not just the sum of residuals?
think.a: For the OLS line, positive and negative residuals always cancel: Σeᵢ = 0. Squaring makes every error count and penalises large errors more.

theory.title: Interpreting slope, intercept and predictions
theory.outcome: Interpret b₀ and b₁ in context and make (sensible) predictions.
theory.why: An exam question rarely stops at the numbers — "interpret the slope" is a classic.
theory.definition:
- **Slope** b₁: the estimated **average** change in Y for a one-unit increase in X.
- **Intercept** b₀: the estimated mean of Y when X = 0 — only meaningful if X = 0 lies within the data range.
- **Prediction**: $\hat y = b_0 + b_1 x_0$. **Residual**: $e = y - \hat y$.
- **Extrapolation** (x₀ far outside the observed range) is unreliable.
theory.example: GPA = 10 + 0.8 × hours of study per day. Slope: each additional daily study hour is associated with a GPA that is on average 0.8 points higher. For 6 h: ŷ = 10 + 0.8·6 = **14.8**. A student with 6 h and GPA 16 has residual 16 − 14.8 = +1.2.
mistakes: "GPA increases by 0.8" without "on average / estimated".
Interpreting the intercept when x = 0 is far outside the data.
Predicting for 20 h/day — extrapolation.
theory.examTip: Slope template: "For each additional [unit of X], [Y] is estimated to change by b₁ [units of Y] on average."

theory.title: Goodness of fit: SST = SSR + SSE and R²
theory.outcome: Decompose the variability of Y and compute and interpret R² and the standard error of the estimate.
theory.why: Same idea as ANOVA: how much of the variability of Y does the line explain?
theory.definition:
- SST = Σ(y − ȳ)²: total; SSR = Σ(ŷ − ȳ)²: explained by the regression; SSE = Σ(y − ŷ)²: unexplained.
- **R² = SSR/SST = 1 − SSE/SST**: share of the variability of Y explained by the linear model; in simple regression R² = r².
- **Standard error of the estimate** $s_e = \sqrt{SSE/(n-2)}$: typical size of a residual, in units of Y.
theory.example: R² = 0.60: 60 % of the variability of GPA is explained by daily study hours; 40 % is due to other factors. Then r = +√0.60 = 0.775 (sign from the slope).
mistakes: R² = 0.60 → "the prediction is 60 % accurate" — wrong.
r = √R² without taking the sign of b₁.
theory.examTip: R² sentence: "[R²·100] % of the variability in [Y] is explained by the linear relationship with [X]."

theory.title: Inference on the slope: t test and confidence interval
theory.outcome: Test H₀: β₁ = 0 with a t test (df = n − 2) and build a CI for β₁.
theory.why: A sample slope of 0.8 could appear by chance even if X and Y are unrelated in the population.
theory.definition:
- $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ (no linear relationship) vs $H_1: \beta_1 \ne 0$.
- $t = \frac{b_1 - 0}{s_{b_1}}$ with $s_{b_1} = \frac{s_e}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}$, df = **n − 2**.
- Reject if |t| > $t_{1-\alpha/2;\,n-2}$.
- CI: $b_1 \pm t_{1-\alpha/2;\,n-2}\, s_{b_1}$. If 0 is outside the CI → reject H₀.
mistakes: Using df = n − 1 (one parameter) — regression estimates two: df = n − 2.
Testing b₁ = 0 (sample) instead of β₁ = 0 (population).
theory.examTip: In Excel output the slope row gives Coefficient, Standard Error, t Stat, P-value, Lower 95%, Upper 95% — read them, don't recompute.

theory.title: The regression ANOVA table and F = t²
theory.outcome: Read and complete the regression ANOVA table and link F and t.
theory.why: Software prints an ANOVA table for every regression. In simple regression it tests exactly the same thing as the slope t test.
theory.definition:
- Regression row: SSR, df 1, MSR = SSR/1.
- Residual row: SSE, df n − 2, MSE = SSE/(n − 2).
- Total: SST, df n − 1.
- $F = MSR/MSE \sim F_{1,\,n-2}$; in simple regression $F = t^2$ and both p-values are identical.
mistakes: Using df (1, n − 1) for F — the denominator is n − 2.
Thinking F and t can give different decisions in simple regression.
theory.examTip: "Significance F" in Excel = p-value of the F test.

theory.title: Assumptions, residuals and causation
theory.outcome: Check the regression assumptions with residual plots and avoid causal over-interpretation.
theory.why: Inference (t, F, CIs) is only trustworthy when the model assumptions hold.
theory.definition:
- **LINE**: Linearity, Independence of errors, Normality of errors, Equal variance (homoscedasticity).
- Residual plot (e vs x or ŷ): should be a structureless band around 0. A curve → non-linearity; a funnel → heteroscedasticity.
- Outliers and influential points can change the line a lot.
- **Correlation/regression ≠ causation**: confounders (e.g. motivation drives both study hours and grades).
theory.example: Grade vs. study hours: residuals scatter evenly around 0 → assumptions plausible. But motivated students study more **and** perform better — the slope is not a causal effect.
mistakes: Checking normality of X instead of the residuals.
"Studying 1 h more causes 4.5 more points."
theory.examTip: Exam favourite: name one assumption and how to check it (residual plot / histogram of residuals).
